passages.text: Sirs — I write to you on a matter of some urgency regarding the condition of the schoolroom on Barton Lane. The windows have not been repaired since the storm of October last, and the children sit in coats and gloves through the morning lessons. The stove, which formerly provided adequate warmth, has been condemned by the inspector and not replaced. I do not write to complain for its own sake. I write because the attendance register shows a steady decline, and the parents of this parish will not send their children to a room where they cannot hold a pen for the cold. I trust you will act before the winter worsens.
passages.label: Source A — A Letter to the School Board, 1887

passages.text: We like to talk about curriculum reform and teacher training, but nobody wants to discuss the leak in the ceiling. I visited three schools last month — two primaries and a secondary — and in every one, staff pointed to something broken that had been broken for years. A window that won't close. A heating system from the 1990s held together with optimism. One head teacher told me she'd stopped reporting the damp because the forms took longer than the repair. There's a quiet resignation in schools about their buildings, as though crumbling plaster is just part of the job. It shouldn't be. If we expect students to take their education seriously, we should take their environment seriously too.
passages.label: Source B — Blog Post: Why School Buildings Still Matter

passages.text: The dwellings of the labouring poor in the district of Millford present a spectacle which no civilised nation ought to tolerate. In one court, measuring not above thirty feet in breadth, I counted eleven separate households, the refuse of which is deposited in a common channel running through the centre. The air is thick with the smell of decay. The inhabitants, when questioned, expressed no surprise at the prevalence of fever among their children, for they have known no other condition. It is the opinion of this committee that the connection between sanitary neglect and disease is no longer a matter of speculation but of established fact, and that the responsibility for improvement lies not with the poor themselves but with those who govern.
passages.label: Source C — Extract from a Report on Public Health, 1848

passages.text: The traveller who ventures beyond the manufacturing towns will discover a country of remarkable beauty and stubborn character. The roads, though improved in recent years, remain narrow in the upland districts, and the inns, while clean, offer little in the way of luxury. One must carry provisions for the day, for the distances between villages are not to be underestimated. The people of these parts are hospitable but reserved, and the visitor should not mistake their silence for unfriendliness. It is simply the manner of those who have spent their lives in the company of sheep and stone walls rather than drawing rooms.
passages.label: Source A — A Guide for Travellers to the North, 1862

passages.text: Ladies and gentlemen — I stand before you this evening to speak not of grand buildings or fine architecture, but of something altogether more powerful: the free circulation of knowledge. A library is not a monument. It is a tool. And like any tool, its value lies not in its appearance but in the hands that use it. Consider the young clerk who walks past these doors each morning. He has no fortune, no connections, no university behind him. But give him access to the shelves within, and you give him the means to educate himself, to rise, to contribute. We do not build libraries for the wealthy. They have their own. We build them for those who have nothing but ambition and a willingness to learn.
passages.label: Source B — A Speech on Public Libraries, 1876

passages.text: My Lord — I have completed my inspection of the cotton mills in the valley of Thornden, and I must report what I have witnessed with a candour that I hope will not cause offence. In the lower mill, children of eight and nine years are employed at the spinning frames from six in the morning until half past seven in the evening, with one interval of thirty minutes for their dinner. Their faces are pale and their bodies thin. Several bore marks upon their hands where the machinery had caught them. When I inquired of the overlooker whether the children were well, he replied that they were 'used to it.' I confess that this phrase has haunted me since. To be used to suffering is not the same as to be well. I urge your Lordship to consider whether a nation that permits such conditions can call itself just.
passages.label: Source C — A Letter from a Factory Inspector, 1843

The park, which occupies the site of the former Greenfield Brickworks, has been planted with elm and lime trees along its central avenue, and a bandstand of wrought iron stands at its eastern end. Benches have been placed at intervals along the paths. The Mayor, in his address, expressed the hope that the park would serve as a place of rest and recreation for the working families of the district, many of whom have no garden of their own. He noted that the land had been donated by the estate of the late Mr Alderman Whitfield, who had long advocated for open spaces in the borough.

passages.text: Somewhere between the safety inspections and the rubberised surfaces, we lost the point of playgrounds. I remember climbing trees in a park that had actual mud. Now everything is colour-coded, padded, and designed by a committee that has clearly never met a child. The swings have been replaced by a 'sensory exploration zone,' which is a plastic dome with holes in it. Children stand around it looking baffled. Meanwhile, the one piece of equipment they actually use — a battered old climbing frame — is earmarked for removal because it doesn't meet current guidelines. I'm not arguing for danger. I'm arguing for the understanding that a scraped knee is not a scandal, and that children learn more from risk than from rubber.

passages.text: It is a truth acknowledged by physicians and clergymen alike that the health of the labouring population is intimately connected with the provision of open air and wholesome recreation. The crowded courts and alleys in which the working man passes his few leisure hours offer no relief from the confinement of the factory or the workshop. A public garden, however modest, provides what these confined spaces cannot: light, air, and the restorative influence of nature upon the mind and body. We do not propose extravagance. A few acres of planted ground, with walks and seats and shade, would answer the purpose. But we propose it urgently, for the alternative — a population weakened in body and debased in spirit — is a cost that no borough can afford.

passages.text: Nobody teaches you how to queue. You just absorb it, the way you absorb table manners or the understanding that you don't make eye contact on the Tube. And yet the queue is one of the most structurally sophisticated social performances we engage in. Consider what it requires. You must identify the end of the line — not always obvious — and position yourself at an appropriate distance from the person ahead. Too close and you're threatening. Too far and someone will step into the gap. You must then remain still without appearing rigid, occupied without appearing distracted. You must not speak to the person ahead of you unless the wait exceeds twenty minutes, at which point a single comment about the wait itself becomes acceptable. And through all of this, you must pretend that none of it is effort. The queue demands constant social calibration disguised as doing nothing.

We are told that attendance will be made compulsory. Very well. But how will the families of the poorest children survive the loss of their labour? steps.content: The phrase 'never again be quite as far from anywhere' is a double negative that the reader has to unpick. This grammatical complexity forces the reader to slow down and think about the meaning — the town's isolation has ended permanently.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The writer structures the final sentence as a progression from quick, physical actions to a slow, reflective observation about permanent change. The shift from simple clauses to a complex subordinate clause mirrors the shift from the event itself to its historical significance — the railway has changed the town forever.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: The two short sentences beginning 'Too close... Too far...' use parallel structure — the same grammatical pattern repeated. This creates a sense of impossible precision, as though the writer is describing a scientific procedure rather than standing in a queue.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: The balanced opposites ('still without appearing rigid, occupied without appearing distracted') create antithesis. The humour comes from the gap between how trivial the situation is (a queue) and how complex the writer makes it sound.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: The structural escalation throughout the paragraph — from simple observation to increasingly detailed 'rules' — builds comic tension. Each new sentence adds another absurd requirement, and the cumulative effect is the joke.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The writer uses parallel structures, balanced antitheses, and structural escalation to make queuing sound absurdly complicated. The humour lies in the contrast between the trivial subject and the formal, analytical sentence structures — the writer describes doing nothing as though it were a performance art.

passages.text: Riverside Community Garden needs your help. Every Saturday morning, a small group of volunteers meets to tend the raised beds, clear paths, and keep the garden open for everyone in the neighbourhood. No experience is necessary — we'll teach you everything you need to know. You don't need your own tools, and you certainly don't need green fingers. What you do need is a spare couple of hours and the willingness to get your hands dirty. In return, you'll learn new skills, meet good people, and leave feeling like you've done something that matters. Tea and biscuits provided. Interested? Drop in any Saturday between nine and twelve, or email volunteer@riverside-garden.org.
passages.label: Source A — Leaflet: Volunteering at Riverside Community Garden

passages.text: You know you should get more sleep. Everyone knows they should get more sleep. The problem is that knowing and doing are separated by a screen, a to-do list, and the comforting lie that you'll catch up at the weekend. You won't. Sleep debt doesn't work like a bank account. You can't deposit eight hours on Sunday and withdraw three on Wednesday. What you can do is small, boring things that actually work. Go to bed at the same time every night. Yes, even on Fridays. Dim the lights an hour before bed — your phone counts as a light, by the way. And stop telling yourself you function fine on six hours. You don't. You've just forgotten what rested feels like.
passages.label: Source B — Health Column: What Nobody Tells You About Sleep

passages.text: Gentlemen — It has come to my attention that the Corporation proposes to sell the woodland known as Stanton Copse for the purpose of building. I write to urge you, in the strongest terms, to reconsider. This wood is not merely an ornament. It is the last remaining fragment of ancient forest in the parish, and its loss would be irreversible. The oaks that stand there were old when our grandfathers were children. They provide shelter for birds that nest nowhere else in the district. They clean the air that blows over the town. They give shade and beauty and quietness to those who walk among them. Once felled, they cannot be replaced in our lifetimes, nor in our children's lifetimes. I ask you to consider what you would say to the generations that follow, if they should ask what became of the trees.
passages.label: Source C — A Letter Urging the Preservation of Woodland, 1889

method_card.title: Purpose: Persuade, Inform, and Advise
method_card.content: Non-fiction texts have purposes — to persuade, inform, advise, describe, explain, or instruct. Most texts blend multiple purposes. Identifying the dominant purpose and how language serves it is essential for Component 1 Reading questions.

exam_context.time: Purpose awareness should underpin every answer, not just one question
exam_context.marks: Understanding purpose links to AO1 and AO3 — worth up to 12 marks across questions
exam_context.frequency: Every Component 1 text is designed for a specific purpose and audience — this is always assessed.

gold.context: A good response analyses: 'not merely an ornament' as redefinition (the wood has practical and historical value); 'old when our grandfathers were children' as an emotional time-scale argument; the tricolon 'shade and beauty and quietness' appealing to aesthetic and emotional values; 'irreversible' as a key persuasive word (no second chance); and the closing rhetorical question about future generations as a guilt-based appeal that makes the reader responsible for posterity.

passages.text: The management of a household requires as much skill and forethought as the management of a business, though it is seldom valued as such. The mistress of the house must rise early, for the morning hours are the most productive. She must see that the fires are laid, the breakfast prepared, the children dressed and sent to school. She must keep accounts of every penny spent, for a household that does not know its expenses cannot govern them. She must inspect the larder, plan the meals for the week, and ensure that nothing is wasted — for waste is the enemy of comfort. Above all, she must maintain a cheerful and orderly home, for the temper of a household is set by the temper of its mistress.
passages.label: Source A — A Guide to Domestic Economy, 1865

passages.text: The phrase 'mental load' entered popular conversation around 2017, but the reality it describes is as old as households themselves. Someone has to remember that the bins go out on Thursday. Someone has to notice that the school shoes are too small before the child complains. Someone has to hold the calendar in their head — the dentist appointment, the parents' evening, the permission slip due tomorrow. This work is invisible because it doesn't produce anything you can point to. Nobody thanks you for remembering to buy milk before it runs out. The house just continues to function, and everyone assumes it does so on its own. What we're really talking about, of course, is planning. And planning is work, even if it happens in your head rather than at a desk.
passages.label: Source B — Online Article: The Invisible Labour of Running a Home, 2022

passages.text: The decline in the number of young women entering domestic service has been remarked upon in every quarter, and the cause is not difficult to discover. The factory and the shop offer what the household cannot: fixed hours, defined duties, and the company of equals. A servant in a private house works from dawn until her employer retires for the night. Her duties are as various as the needs of the family, and her hours of rest are determined not by the clock but by the whims of those she serves. Small wonder, then, that the more spirited among them prefer the mill, where the work is hard but the evening is their own. We shall not reverse this trend by lamenting it. We shall reverse it only by improving the conditions of service until they bear some resemblance to the conditions we now expect in every other form of employment.
passages.label: Source C — A Pamphlet on the Employment of Domestic Servants, 1891

method_card.title: Summarising and Synthesising
method_card.content: Summarising means identifying the key ideas in a single text and expressing them concisely. Synthesising means drawing together information from two or more texts to identify connections, contrasts, and patterns. Both skills require you to be selective — not everything in the text belongs in your summary.

exam_context.time: Allow 8-10 minutes — planning which points to include saves time

exam_context.frequency: Summarising and synthesising across texts is tested in every Component 1 paper.

passages.text: When Margaret Osei opens the shutters of Chapters Bookshop each morning, she counts the other shops that are still dark. The bakery closed in January. The florist lasted until March. The phone-repair place, which had seemed immune to everything, put its lease up last week. Margaret has run Chapters for twenty-two years, and in that time the high street has lost its post office, its bank, and most of its reasons for people to visit. She does not blame the internet, exactly. She blames the feeling that nobody fights for places like this anymore. On Saturday mornings, a queue still forms before she unlocks the door. The people in it know each other’s names.
passages.label: Source A — Newspaper Column: The Last Bookshop on the High Street

passages.text: Dear Members of the Planning Committee, We write to you not as campaigners, but as parents, teachers, and residents who remember what this land used to be. Thirty years ago, every child at Ashfield Primary had access to two full-sized playing fields, a long-jump pit, and a nature garden maintained by volunteers. Today, the remaining field is waterlogged for six months of the year because the drainage was removed during the last round of building work. The proposal before you would concrete over the final green space to create a car park for the new medical centre. We understand the need for healthcare provision. But we also understand that children who have nowhere to run at lunchtime do not sit quietly and learn all afternoon. They climb walls. They fight. They stare out of windows. We ask you to consider whether a community that paves over its children’s play space has truly weighed up the cost.
passages.label: Source B — Open Letter: Save Our School Playing Fields

passages.text: Visited the Marsden brothers’ mill at half past six this morning and found the gates already open, which is to say the children were already inside. The youngest I counted was a girl of eight or nine, though her mother swore she was ten. She stood at the spinning frame with her arms stretched wide, and I noticed her fingers were wrapped in rags where the thread had cut them. The overseer, a Mr Caldwell, followed me through the mill with great courtesy, pointing out the ventilation shafts and the new guard-rails on the machines as though I were a visitor to a country house being shown the gardens. When I asked how many hours the children worked, he said ten, which the children’s faces did not confirm. I made my notes. I said nothing that could be quoted. I left knowing that my report would change nothing this year, and perhaps not the next.
passages.label: Source C — Diary of a Factory Inspector, 1843

method_card.title: Drawing Inferences and Using Evidence
method_card.content: Inference means reading between the lines — working out what a writer suggests without stating it directly. Strong inference is always anchored to evidence: a specific word, phrase, or detail from the text that supports your reading. In non-fiction, writers use tone, word choice, and selective detail to guide the reader toward conclusions they never spell out.

Funding from the council has been cut by forty per cent, and the cost of feeding and housing our animals has risen sharply. Without your help, the gates will close in March. passages.text: There are those who argue that the working man needs no education beyond what his trade requires. We have heard this argument from mill owners, from Members of Parliament, and from gentlemen who themselves enjoyed the finest schooling this country can offer. It is a convenient belief for those who benefit from a population that cannot read a contract, question a wage, or write a letter to a newspaper. We do not suggest that every labourer should study Greek. But we do suggest that a man who can read is a man who can think, and a man who can think is a man who cannot be so easily governed. This, we suspect, is the true objection to working-class education — not that it is unnecessary, but that it is dangerous. Dangerous, that is, to those who prefer their workers quiet and their voters ignorant.

passages.text: I deleted my social media accounts six months ago and I have not missed them once. The first week was strange — I kept reaching for my phone at traffic lights, in queues, during the adverts. But by the second week, I started noticing things I had stopped seeing: the colour of the sky at six in the morning, the conversations happening around me in cafes, the fact that my daughter talks to me more when I am not scrolling. I am not saying everyone should do this. I am saying that I did not realise how much of my attention I had given away until I took it back. My friends think I am being dramatic. Maybe I am. But I sleep better, I read more, and I have not compared my life to a stranger’s highlight reel in one hundred and eighty-two days.

passages.text: Every few months, someone writes an article about quitting social media as though they have discovered fire. They describe the newfound peace, the birdsong, the books they have finally read. What they do not mention is the privilege of disconnection. Not everyone can afford to step away. For millions of people, social media is not a distraction — it is a lifeline. It is the disabled person whose only daily social contact is an online support group. It is the small-business owner whose entire livelihood depends on Instagram. It is the teenager in a village with no youth club who finds community in a group chat. The problem with social media is not social media. It is the same problem we have always had: some people use tools well and others use them badly. Blaming the tool is easier than examining the user.

passages.text: Sir, I write in response to your correspondent who celebrated the spread of penny newspapers among the working classes. That a man may now buy a newspaper for the price of a loaf is, I am told, progress. I confess I see it differently. The penny press does not educate; it excites. It fills the mind with sensation and scandal where there might otherwise be silence and thought. A man who reads nothing is at least free to observe the world with his own eyes. A man who reads the penny press sees the world through the eyes of the editor, and mistakes that borrowed sight for his own understanding. I do not object to the working man reading. I object to what he is given to read. The remedy is not fewer newspapers but better ones — and that, I fear, is a remedy no one wishes to fund.

passages.text: There is no sport more honest than five-a-side football. No coaches, no substitutes, no VAR. Just ten people, a concrete pitch, and a ball that has been kicked so many times it barely bounces. Every Tuesday evening, we gather at the leisure centre at the edge of town. There are teachers, plumbers, a retired accountant, and a seventeen-year-old who runs rings around all of us. Nobody keeps score, or rather, everybody keeps a different score. The tackles are reckless. The passing is hopeful at best. And for one hour a week, nobody checks their phone, worries about their mortgage, or remembers that they are forty-three years old and should probably warm up first. It is, in every sense, a beautiful mess.
passages.label: Source A — Sports Column: The Beautiful Chaos of Five-a-Side

passages.text: Last Christmas, over four thousand people slept in emergency shelters run by volunteers. They were not the people you might expect. They were former teachers, ex-soldiers, grandparents who had lost their homes after a single missed payment. Nobody plans to spend Christmas in a sleeping bag on a church floor. But for thousands of people every year, that is the reality. A hot meal costs us three pounds to provide. A bed for the night costs twelve. A conversation with a trained support worker — the kind of conversation that can change the direction of a life — costs nothing, because our workers give their time for free. This Christmas, we are not asking you to solve homelessness. We are asking you to make one night warmer.
passages.label: Source B — Charity Website: Crisis at Christmas

passages.text: I have visited the mills. I have seen the children. I have watched a boy of seven carry bobbins from six in the morning until eight at night, and I have seen him fall asleep standing at his frame, and be struck to wake him. Honourable members will tell me that the trade must have its hands, and that the hands must be small. They will tell me that the parents consent, as though consent given under the threat of starvation is consent at all. They will tell me that the children are fed, as though feeding a child you have worked to exhaustion is an act of kindness. I am not here to propose the end of industry. I am here to propose that industry should not require the destruction of childhood.
passages.label: Source C — Parliamentary Speech on Child Labour, 1833

method_card.title: Using Linguistic Terminology
method_card.content: Linguistic terminology means the precise names for the language features writers use: metaphor, rhetorical question, emotive language, anaphora, and so on. Using the right term shows the examiner you can identify techniques. But naming a technique alone is not enough — you must always explain its effect on the reader.

exam_context.marks: Language analysis questions worth up to 12 marks
exam_context.frequency: Accurate use of linguistic terminology is rewarded across all reading questions in Component 1.

gold.context: A good response analyses: ‘I have visited… I have seen… I have watched’ (anaphora establishing the speaker as a witness with moral authority), ‘They will tell me… They will tell me… They will tell me’ (anaphora pre-empting opponents’ arguments to dismantle them), and the parallel structure of ‘as though consent given under the threat of starvation is consent at all’ / ‘as though feeding a child you have worked to exhaustion is an act of kindness’ (redefining opponents’ terms against them).

The technique is the same but the purposes are opposite: one creates joy, the other creates outrage. Context matters: a sports column aims to entertain, a parliamentary speech aims to change law.

The juxtaposition of ‘industry’ and ‘childhood’ forces the listener to weigh economic gain against human cost.

statements.text: Metaphor: a direct comparison saying something IS something else.
statements.explain: A metaphor states that one thing IS another (e.g., ‘it is a beautiful mess’).

statements.text: Simile: a comparison that says something is LIKE something else.
statements.explain: Similes use ‘like’ or ‘as’ to compare.

statements.text: Anaphora: ending sentences with the same word.
statements.explain: Anaphora is the repetition of a word or phrase at the BEGINNING of successive clauses or sentences, not the end.

statements.text: Rhetorical question: a question asked for effect, not expecting an answer.
statements.explain: Rhetorical questions make the reader think rather than demanding a reply.

statements.text: Hyperbole: deliberate exaggeration for emphasis.
statements.explain: Hyperbole overstates something to create a strong impression.

statements.text: Emotive language: words chosen to trigger an emotional response.
statements.explain: Emotive language is designed to make the reader feel something — sympathy, anger, hope.

steps.content: The writer uses a list (asyndetic listing) of different professions and ages. Name the technique precisely: this is listing used to show variety within a group.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: The effect is to show that five-a-side brings together people who would not normally mix. The range of occupations and ages creates a sense of an unlikely community.

The final detail, that the youngest player ‘runs rings around all of us,’ adds self-deprecating humour and positions the group as equal on the pitch despite their differences off it.

steps.content: This is a tricolon (rule of three) where each item escalates: meal, bed, conversation. The costs move from small to zero, but the value increases.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: The final item breaks the expected pattern. After financial costs (three pounds, twelve pounds), we expect a higher figure. Instead, the most valuable thing — a conversation — costs nothing. This subversion makes it more powerful.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: The parenthetical clause ‘the kind of conversation that can change the direction of a life’ interrupts the rhythm to emphasise the emotional weight of what volunteers provide.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The tricolon builds from practical needs (meal, bed) to emotional support (conversation), with costs descending from three pounds to nothing. The climactic third item subverts the pattern: the most transformative thing is free. The parenthetical interruption (‘the kind that can change the direction of a life’) slows the reader down at the most important point, ensuring the emotional impact lands.

passages.text: I’ll be honest: I came to the Lake District expecting postcards. Rolling hills, stone walls, the sort of landscape you see on shortbread tins. And I got all of that, obviously. But what I didn’t expect was how physical it would be. By the end of day one, my legs felt like they belonged to someone else. Helvellyn nearly finished me off — the wind at the top was brutal, and the path along Striding Edge is not, as the guidebook cheerfully claims, ‘suitable for confident walkers.’ It is suitable for mountain goats and people who enjoy the possibility of death. But the view from the summit, with the clouds pulling apart below you and the lakes shining like spilt silver, was worth every terrified step. Would I go back? Already booked.

We are not pacifists who refuse to see danger. We are parents, teachers, doctors, and students who refuse to accept that the annihilation of civilisation is a reasonable price for political strategy. If you believe that your children deserve to grow up, join us. If you believe that one country’s pride is not worth another country’s existence, join us. method_card.title: Context and Genre in Non-Fiction
method_card.content: Understanding context means knowing when, where, and why a text was written, and how that shapes its meaning. Understanding genre means recognising the conventions of the text type — a diary reads differently from a speech, a letter from an editorial. The best readers use context and genre to explain why a writer makes the choices they do, not just what those choices are.

passages.text: Plans to build a bypass around the market town of Hartwell have split the community. The proposed road, which would divert through-traffic away from the high street, has the backing of local businesses who say lorries and congestion are killing trade. Graham Whitfield, who runs the town’s hardware shop, said: ‘You can’t push a pram down the pavement without being clipped by a wing mirror. It’s not a high street anymore, it’s a motorway.’ But residents on the eastern edge of town, where the road would be built, are furious. A petition signed by over two thousand people argues the bypass would destroy farmland, increase noise pollution, and cut the village of Lower Hartwell off from the rest of the community. Local farmer Janet Barlow said: ‘They’re not building a bypass. They’re building a wall between neighbours.’ The council will vote on the proposal next month.

passages.text: I know what you are thinking. Libraries are old-fashioned. Everything is online now. Why would anyone walk into a building to borrow a book when they can download one in three seconds? I will tell you why. Because a library is not a book shop with free stock. It is the only public space left where you do not have to buy something to sit down. It is where the retired man comes every morning because his flat is too quiet. It is where the teenager does her homework because her house is too loud. It is where the mother and toddler group meets because the church hall charges forty pounds an hour. Close a library and you do not just remove books. You remove the last place in a community where people can simply be, without being sold to, moved on, or charged for the privilege. We are not asking for more money. We are asking you to stop taking it away.

passages.text: The factory stood at the end of our street like a great brick church, and we were its congregation. Every morning at half past five the hooter sounded, and the doors opened, and the women and children filed in as though answering a call to prayer. I was nine when I began, and I thought myself fortunate, for my mother had begun at seven. My work was to carry the unfired plates from the moulding bench to the kiln, a distance of perhaps thirty yards, though it felt like thirty miles by the end of the day. The heat from the kiln dried the sweat on your face before you could wipe it. The older women sang while they worked, songs I did not understand then but which I have never forgotten. In the evening I sat with my mother at our kitchen table and she taught me letters from a newspaper she had found in the yard. She said that reading was the only door that nobody could lock.
passages.label: Source C — Memoir: A Childhood in the Potteries, 1880
